entries.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
entries.content:
ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF

Image-Text-to-Text • 177B • Updated • 7.44M • 1.32k

180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Update on GitHub

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with 

llama.app
on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through 
pi
. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

What is Strata?

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

How do other engines offload?

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with 

mmap
and can keep the experts on the CPU (
--cpu-moe
, 
--n-cpu-moe N
, 
-ot "exps=CPU"
, or 
--fit on
to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (
--moe-cache-mib
) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's 

--cpu-offload-gb N
puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; 
--cpu-offload-params experts
keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (

device_map="auto"
, 
offload_folder
), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before 
forward
. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

EngineDecode (tok/s)
Strata, Q8_082 - 88
llama.cpp, Q8_0, 
--fit on
 63 - 64
llama.cpp, BF16, 
--fit on
 35 - 36
vLLM, FP8, 
--cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts
 20.1
vLLM, FP8, same flags, 
--enforce-eager
 14.7
vLLM, FP8, 
--cpu-offload-gb 16
 9.7
vLLM, BF16, 
--cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts
 7.3
vLLM, BF16, 
--cpu-offload-gb 50
 3.3
Transformers + Accelerate0.16

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

Start small

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses 

grouped_mm
, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so 

grouped_mm
runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

experts_offload

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of 

from_pretrained
, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:
pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head"

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

path = snapshot_download("tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming")

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    f"{path}/dense",
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map={"": "mps", "experts.*": "disk"},
    quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits=8),
    experts_offload={
        "cache_bytes": 12 << 30,
        "quantized_experts": f"{path}/experts-q3",
    },
)

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to 

"disk"
go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The 

device_map
form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

  • experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device
  • dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16)
  • the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

TransformersStrataGap
Decode, 200 tokens10.0 tok/s14.81.5x
Prefill, 4K prompt68 tok/s2203.2x
Decode after a 6K document7.3 tok/s13.71.9x

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Closing the gap

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

  • Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch.
  • Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections.
  • Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights, reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size.
  • Prefill, we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed.
  • Long documents: attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token.
  • Misses: Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

TransformersStrataGap
Decode, 200 tokens13.9 tok/s14.81.06x
Prefill, 4K prompt228 tok/s2201.0x
Decode after a 6K document12.4 tok/s13.71.1x

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

Conclusion

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that 

grouped_mm
runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with 
torch.mps.compile_shader
, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

entries.title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
entries.content:
Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash

Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.5B • Updated • 1.77k • 193

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Update on GitHub

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

  • Runs anywhere: native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code
  • 40+ languages: automatic language detection
  • Output control: numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language
  • Extremely fast: an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches
  • Holds up on real phone calls: on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark

Quickstart

Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers

uv pip install torch transformers accelerate

from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM

model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")

inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(
    audio="https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3",
    language="English",  # omit to detect automatically
).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype)

output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=512)
generated = output[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]:]
print(processor.decode(generated, return_format="transcription_only")[0])  # return_format="parsed" if detecting language


audio
accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

How it's built

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or 

trust_remote_code
.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

Results

Accuracy for its size

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Speed

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Real phone calls

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

Try it

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

entries.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Run them with the tools you already use

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

How open-weight models are used

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Routing powered by OpenRouter

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

zai-org/GLM-5.3            # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability
zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest    # highest throughput
zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest   # lowest price
zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita     # only Novita

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the 

X-HF-Session-Id
header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video and audio generation

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

See where your requests go

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Breaking change: custom provider keys

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (

model:provider
) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

What's next

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

  • Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face.
  • More tasks routed through OpenRouter.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

entries.title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
entries.content:
Robotiq-Official/simready-assets

Viewer • Updated • 4 • 5.37k • 2

Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

Enterprise + Article

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

What makes a robot asset SimReady?

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

  • Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body.
  • Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled.
  • Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

What comes with the asset, and what do you add?

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

What should you check before running a pick-and-place task?

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

  • Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings.
  • Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper.
  • Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Required Software:

  • Install Isaac Sim 6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements.
  • Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Install the Hugging Face CLI only if you choose the command-line asset download option.
  • Use the USD Search endpoint.

Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

What does asset validation tell you?

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

Sample prompt used in this example:

Assemble the robot arm 
with the gripper 
using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim
https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html.

Validate the assembly on completion.

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Sample prompt used in this example:

Run pick and place with the assembled robot and soda can
 in Isaac Sim.

Ensure you do a contact based grasp for picking up the can and validate
the accuracy/placement error for the pick and place as well.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

Simulation assumptions:

  • Fixed setup: The can starts at a known position, with an anchored robot and clear, flat workspace. No vision was used and collision checks were limited.
  • Simplified can: Deformation and liquid motion are not modeled, so this example does not test crushing.
  • Scripted grasp and motion: A horizontal grasp uses a 2 N·m drive-effort cap chosen through simulation tests, not calibrated to fingertip forces or recommended by the manufacturer. Contact and friction hold the beverage can as the arm follows fixed waypoints without replanning. For hardware gripping-force specifications, see the Robotiq product sheet.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your next simulation with SimReady Assets

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

Discover assets

  • Find robots and objects: Browse SimReady Central on Hugging Face.
  • Check what an asset supports: Review the profiles and requirements in SimReady Foundation alongside the asset’s validation reports.

Build a pick-and-place scene

  • Set up the simulator: Follow the Isaac Sim installation guide for the version used in this example.
  • Connect your agent: Follow the Isaac Sim Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Assemble the robot: Follow the Robot Assembler tutorial if you prefer to connect the arm and gripper manually.

Prepare and contribute content

  • Start from CAD: Follow the 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics to prepare your own robotics assets.
  • Validate and submit assets: Follow the SimReady Central submission guide to make your assets available to other developers.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

Happy building!

entries.title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
entries.content:
allenai/XYBench-dataset

Viewer • Updated • 11.3k • 998 • 3

XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Enterprise Article

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

Building XYBench

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

Evaluating how an answer helps

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

  • Pragmatic solution—records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately.
  • Pragmatic emphasis—measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two.
  • Misconception identification—measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y).

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

What the experiments show

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

What this means for evaluation

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.
